title: Design a payment system.
description: Idempotent money movement: authorization/capture, double-entry ledger, reconciliation with providers, and failure-safe state machines.

data.text: **Question:** Design a payment system that charges customers, tracks money movement, and never double-charges.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Charge a card via a provider (Stripe/Adyen), support refunds and partial captures
Exactly-once charging despite client retries, timeouts, and webhooks
Full audit trail: every state transition recorded, money provable
Reconcile our state with the provider's authoritative state
Support multiple providers with failover routing
PCI scope minimized: never store raw card data

data.caption: Payment service between the app and providers, with idempotency, webhooks, and reconciliation
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[App - idempotency key] --> B[Payment API]
    B --> C[(Payments DB - state machine)]
    B --> D[Provider Router]
    D --> E[Stripe]
    D --> F[Adyen]
    G[Provider Webhooks] --> H[Webhook Processor]
    H --> C
    I[Reconciliation Job] --> C
    I --> E
    I --> F
    C --> J[Ledger - double entry]
    K[Outbox] --> L[Events: PaymentCaptured/Failed]

data.text: The core idea: our **payment intent is a state machine** persisted before touching any provider, driven forward by API responses and webhooks, and **reconciled** against provider truth. Clients pass an **idempotency key**; the provider call passes the same key upstream — so a retry after a timeout returns the original result instead of charging twice.

items: State machine: REQUIRES_ACTION → AUTHORIZED → CAPTURED → (REFUNDED/PARTIALLY_REFUNDED); FAILED and CANCELLED terminal transitions — every transition an append-only audit row
Idempotency three layers: client key → our payment record (unique constraint) → provider idempotency key; same key + same payload = same result, forever

Webhooks are the source of async truth: timeout on the API call ≠ failure — webhook or reconciliation confirms; verify signature, dedupe by event id, process out-of-order events by state-machine validity
Double-entry ledger: every capture/refund writes balanced entries (user balance ↔ revenue ↔ fees ↔ refunds) — the ledger, not the payments table, answers 'where is the money?'
Reconciliation job: periodically diff our records against provider settlement files/API; mismatches go to an ops queue — drift found in days, not in audit
Provider routing: strategy by geography/cost/success-rate; failover on circuit-open; a provider's tokenized card references (PM ids) aren't portable — pin instruments per provider
PCI minimization: hosted fields/tokens only — card data flows client→provider, never our servers
Retries to providers: only with idempotency keys; never blind-retry a charge
Money as integers: store minor units (cents) as integers with explicit currency — floats in payments are a bug generator

data.title: The timeout that double-charges
data.text: App calls provider → network timeout → app retries without an idempotency key → two real charges, one order. This exact bug has shipped in countless startups. The fix is unglamorous and non-negotiable: generate the key once per user intent, persist it before the provider call, and pass it to the provider API.

rows: State machine record; one per user intent
Provider-side artifacts, mapped to our states
entry_id, account, direction, amount, payment_id, created_at
Double-entry; sums to zero per transaction

items: Webhook arrives before API response — state machine accepts valid transitions from either direction
Out-of-order webhooks (captured before authorized) — reject invalid transitions, let reconciliation settle
Partial capture and multi-capture flows — amount accounting on the intent, not the charge
Refund racing a dispute/chargeback — dispute state wins; ledger reflects outcome
Provider outage at capture time — intent stays AUTHORIZED with retry scheduled; never fail-open to 'assume captured'
Currency/rounding: minor units, explicit FX rates recorded on the ledger entry
Idempotency key reused with different payload — reject (409); silent re-use is a correctness hole

items.question: Why a double-entry ledger instead of a balance column?
items.answer: A balance column can drift silently; double-entry is self-checking (every transaction sums to zero) and supports fees, refunds, and multi-party splits without special cases. It's how finance has audited money for centuries.

items.question: How do you handle provider failover for stored cards?
items.answer: Tokens aren't portable across providers. Real options: store with multiple providers at tokenization time, use a vaulting aggregator (like Middesk/Basis theory) within PCI scope, or re-tokenize on next purchase — each has cost/UX trade-offs.

items.question: Synchronous API call vs webhook — which is truth?
items.answer: Neither alone: the API response is an early signal, webhooks are the async authority, reconciliation is the final court. Design the state machine to accept any arrival order.

items.question: How would you test this safely?
items.answer: Provider sandbox modes, deterministic webhook replay fixtures, property tests over the state machine (no transition from REFUNDED to CAPTURED), and reconciliation tests seeded with deliberate drift.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Persist intent + idempotency key BEFORE the provider call; pass the key upstream
State machine driven by API responses and webhooks, any arrival order
Double-entry ledger is the audit-grade source of money truth
Reconciliation with providers finds drift; PCI stays out of scope via tokens
data.takeaway: Payments are a state machine over other people's state machines — idempotency keys and reconciliation are how you stay correct when every network call is a maybe.
